source_note: Mei, Zhang, Li & Yang, 'Mechanical Output and Post-exercise Jump Responses to Percentage-Based, Repetitions-in-Reserve, and Velocity-Based Back-Squat Training in Trained Sprinters: A Randomized Crossover Study', Journal of Sports Science and Medicine (2026) 25:915-933, DOI 10.52082/jssm.2026.915 (19 pages). Full randomized within-participant crossover (18 male 100m sprinters) comparing PBT/RIR/VBT back-squat (80% 1RM, 5 sets x <=5 reps) with bilateral force-plate kinetics + CMJ/SJ force-time responses. NULL primary result (no condition effect on force/impulse/CMJ/SJ) despite different realized volume loads; explicit null-vs-equivalence and monitoring-requires-actuation caveats. Extracted faithfully (not a derivative summary). The source prints ONE numbered-style display equation (positive vertical impulse integral, lines 496-504) in a shifted/custom font that extracts garbled; it is reconstructed in labeled LaTeX and flagged. Other relations (net COM acceleration, RSImod, power, volume load) are unambiguous prose definitions reconstructed as labeled LaTeX and flagged in assumptions. Domain physics (biomechanics/force-time kinetics) matches catalog; strength-and-conditioning context (sprinters), not football-specific. The load-regulation control policies (RIR feedback, VBT velocity-loss governor), force-time measurement pipeline, realized-exposure accounting, and actuation gate are sport-agnostic and isomorphic to GSE's load-governance and mechanical-output layer. No sportsbook lines/spreads/totals/implied odds in source or lifted into GSE.

primitives.name: Compare acute mechanical output + post-exercise jump across PBT/RIR/VBT back-squat

assumptions: The study compares session-level mechanical output during back-squat training and immediate postexercise jump responses among percentage-based (PBT), repetitions-in-reserve (RIR), and velocity-based (VBT) protocols in trained male sprinters, integrating force-plate kinetics during training with CMJ/SJ force-time responses rather than relying on barbell velocity or jump height alone.

primitives.name: PBT limitation: a single 1RM may not reflect day-to-day capacity
primitives.verbatim_quote: a single 1RM assessment may not reflect an athlete's day-to-day capacity
assumptions: Percentage-based training prescribes load relative to 1RM, enabling advance planning and standardized programming, but a single 1RM assessment may not reflect an athlete's day-to-day capacity, and even at the same percentage of 1RM the maximum completable repetitions differ substantially among athletes with different training backgrounds.

primitives.name: Same relative load + rep count = different proximity to task failure

reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this paper is the practical question of whether autoregulating resistance-training load actually changes the acute training stimulus and the immediate explosive-performance decrement that follows it. Mei, Zhang, Li, and Yang, writing in the Journal of Sports Science and Medicine in 2026, note that sprinters need lower-body strength and power but must integrate resistance training without unduly reducing the quality of subsequent sprint, jump, or technical work, and that greater within-set velocity loss accompanies higher lactate, impaired jump performance, and greater neuromuscular fatigue. Percentage-based training prescribes load relative to a one-repetition maximum, but a single 1RM may not reflect day-to-day capacity and the same percentage can represent different proximities to task failure across athletes. Velocity-based training and repetitions-in-reserve offer two autoregulation alternatives, yet the authors observe that different regulation methods do not necessarily produce different training exposures, especially when repetitions per set are capped. The study enrolled 18 trained male 100-meter sprinters, mean age 20.0 years, body mass 74.38 kilograms, back-squat 1RM 150 kilograms, and 100-meter performance 11.03 seconds, in a randomized within-participant crossover with at least 72 hours between trials. Each condition began at 80 percent of 1RM and comprised five sets capped at five repetitions: PBT fixed the load and reps, RIR targeted three repetitions in reserve and adjusted the next-set load by plus or minus five kilograms, and VBT terminated a set at a 20 percent mean concentric velocity loss or five repetitions with load held constant. Bilateral Kistler force plates at 1000 Hz recorded vertical ground-reaction force during squatting and during pre- and post-exercise countermovement and squat jumps, filtered with a fourth-order zero-lag Butterworth at 20 Hz. The recursive theory of mind is the force-time measurement pipeline. Net center-of-mass acceleration was computed by subtracting body weight from total vertical force and dividing by mass, velocity and displacement by successive integration, jump height by the impulse-momentum method with flight-time only for quality control, the modified reactive strength index as jump height divided by time to takeoff, power as force times velocity, and positive vertical impulse as the integral of the rectified net force over each segmented cycle. Session volume load was the sum of external load times completed repetitions. Statistics used linear models with participant fixed effects, clustered robust standard errors, joint F tests, log-scale geometric-mean ratios for skewed force and impulse, Holm pairwise adjustment, and paired Hedges' gz. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the gap between realized exposure and detected effect. VBT produced fewer completed repetitions, a mean difference of -0.94 with Holm-adjusted p of 0.001, and lower session volume load than PBT and RIR, while RIR permitted a higher volume load than PBT; so the monitoring feedback did change behavior. Yet the primary analyses detected no significant overall condition effects on relative peak vertical force, mean positive vertical impulse, CMJ jump height, CMJ modified reactive strength index, or SJ jump height, with p values of 0.348, 0.262, 0.969, 0.894, and 0.740 respectively. The authors are explicit that these null results do not demonstrate the protocols produced the same responses, that with 18 participants the design had 80 percent power only for an omnibus Cohen's f of about 0.31, and that the study was not an equivalence trial. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. The RIR plus-or-minus-five-kilogram feedback rule is a closed-loop load controller; the VBT 20 percent velocity-loss termination is a fatigue-threshold governor; volume load is realized-exposure accounting; the rectified net-force impulse is positive-only mechanical credit; and the central thesis that monitoring confers an advantage only when translated into a meaningful stimulus adjustment is GSE's actuation gate. The outputs are mechanical and jump metrics from force plates; GSE lifts no sportsbook lines, spreads, totals, or implied odds. The kinematics-versus-kinetics caution, that barbell velocity and ground-reaction force need not change in parallel, is GSE's proxy-versus-ground-truth distinction. The broader evidence reinforces the humility: meta-analyses of six studies with 124 participants and four randomized trials with 88 participants found no consistent advantage of velocity-based over percentage-based training for strength, power, or sprint, with pooled squat 1RM differences near three kilograms and standardized effects close to zero, and the long-term benefit of autoregulation, where it exists, appears to arise from the accumulation of repeated exposures rather than a smaller decrement after every session. The practical reading is that a five-repetition cap limited how much the velocity-loss termination rule could modify exposure, particularly when the threshold was not reached before the fifth repetition, so the monitoring signal rarely got the chance to act. The caveats close the account. The realized stimulus was not fully matched across conditions, session-level outcomes were averaged across cycles rather than matched repetition positions, the force-time analysis used complete segmented cycles rather than separate braking and propulsion phases, outcomes were assessed only immediately after training without 24-to-48-hour recovery, lactate, or soreness, and the sample was 18 male sprinters only. The invariant for GSE is to carry the load-regulation control policies and the force-time measurement pipeline while recording the null-versus-equivalence veto, the limited sensitivity, the monitoring-requires-actuation principle, and the kinematics-kinetics decoupling before any quantitative reuse, treating a PASS on a bad comparison as a badge of honor rather than a missed bet.

reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Realized exposure differed: VBT reps -0.94 (CI -1.41..-0.48, Holm p=.001); volume load PBT 3000/RIR 3036/VBT 2893 kg (RIR>PBT +36.11 p=.005; VBT<PBT -106.94 p<.001; VBT<RIR -143.06 p<.001). BUT primary null: rel peak force 1.260/1.207/1.237 x system wt (F=1.123 p=.348), mean pos impulse 400.2/353.2/388.2 N.s (F=1.452 p=.262), CMJ height -0.29/-0.09/-0.27cm (p=.969), RSImod (p=.894), SJ (p=.740). Null != equivalence; n=18 limited sensitivity (f=0.31); not equivalence trial; unmatched stimulus; complete-cycle not phase-specific; immediate-only (no 24-48h/lactate/soreness); male sprinters only. Monitoring value ONLY IF feedback changes load/reps/failure-proximity; barbell kinematics != GRF kinetics. Meta-analyses (Liao 2021 6 studies/124, 1RM MD 3.03kg; Orange 2022 4 RCTs/88, SMD .06/.11/-.10) no consistent VBT>PBT. Zero sportsbook lines lifted.

universal_lens: In trained sprinters, three back-squat load-regulation policies (fixed percentage, repetitions-in-reserve feedback, velocity-loss termination) starting at 80% 1RM with five capped sets produce different realized repetition and volume loads but no detected difference in session-level force-plate mechanical output or immediate CMJ/SJ force-time responses — a null result that does not establish equivalence, illustrating that monitoring confers an advantage only when its feedback meaningfully changes the training stimulus.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats PBT fixed %1RM / RIR target-3 load +/-5kg / VBT 20% velocity-loss-or-5-reps; 18 sprinters 20.0y/74.38kg/1RM 150kg/100m 11.03s crossover >=72h; Kistler 1000Hz Butterworth 20Hz; a_COM=(F_z-mg)/m, RSImod=h/t_takeoff, P=F_z*v, J_pos=integral max(F_z-F_cal,0)dt, volume=sum(load x reps); participant FE/clustered SE/joint F/log geometric ratios/Holm/Hedges gz/ICC(A,3); sensitivity f=0.31; realized VBT reps -0.94 (p=.001), volume PBT 3000/RIR 3036/VBT 2893; primary null force p=.348/impulse p=.262/CMJ p=.969/RSImod p=.894/SJ p=.740; null != equivalence, not equivalence trial, monitoring-requires-actuation, kinematics != kinetics; one printed integral reconstructed (shifted font).
gse_mapping: GSE lifts the RIR closed-loop load controller and VBT velocity-loss fatigue governor as load-governance policies, the force-time pipeline (Newton acceleration, impulse-momentum jump height, RSImod, force-velocity power, rectified impulse) as mechanical-output measurement, volume load as realized-exposure accounting, and the monitoring-requires-actuation principle as its actuation gate; records the null-vs-equivalence veto, limited n=18 sensitivity, unmatched-stimulus and immediate-only caveats, and kinematics-vs-kinetics decoupling as honest limits; all outputs are force-plate mechanical and jump metrics, never sportsbook lines, and a PASS on a bad comparison is a badge of honor.
